# Abstract

This gazetteer presents population series for 655 excavated settlements across the ~265k km² Middle and Lower Dnieper basin from the Upper Palaeolithic (10000BC) to the Golden Horde appanage era (1400AD) [@tolochko1983; @kuza1996; @motsia2007]. The prehistoric and ancient tables cover 52 sites, moving from the mammoth-bone camps of Mezhirich and Kirillovskaya (80 - 160 inhabitants in 10000BC) to the Trypillia BII-CI concentric proto-towns of the Cherkasy-Uman plateau at 3600BC (Talianky at 15k, Maidanetske at 10k and Nebelivka at 9k) and the Scythian forest-steppe hillforts and Greek colonies of 500BC (Pontic Olbia at 15k, Belsk-Gelonus at 12k, Kamenskoye at 6k and Trakhtemyriv at 4,5k) [@videiko2004; @shramko1987; @kryzhitsky1999].

Across the 95 medieval Rus towns and frontier fortresses (1000AD - 1400AD), urban growth peaked in 1200AD under the protection of the Stuhna, Irpin, Ros (Porossia) and Sula (Posullya) rampart lines. Kiev rose from 28k in 1000AD to 50k in 1200AD across 380 ha, flanked by Belgorod (9k), Vyshhorod (7k), Pereyaslavl-Russky (15k), the Chorni Klobuky frontier capital of Torchesk (6k) and the Drevlian centres of Ovruch (4,5k) and Iskorosten (4k). Batu Khan's campaigns of 1239-1240AD devastated the exposed forest-steppe forts and reduced Kiev to 4k in 1250AD (8,5k in 1400AD) and Pereyaslavl to 3,5k (4,5k in 1400AD), whereas the wooded Drevlian towns retained half of their inhabitants and the tribute-paying Bolokhov towns survived intact until Daniel of Galicia's punitive expedition of 1257AD [@ivakin1996; @morgunov2003; @tomashevsky2008].

# Methodology

Across the Middle and Lower Dnieper (~265k km²), archaeological excavations and Rus chronicles document 655 principal settlements between the Upper Palaeolithic (10000BC), the Mongol campaigns of 1239-1240 and the Golden Horde appanage era (1250AD - 1400AD) [@tolochko1983; @kuza1996; @motsia2007].

## Population Estimation from Archaeological Evidence

Population estimates for individual towns and villages draw on excavated site areas, medieval rampart circuits and post-Mongol destruction layers.

For prehistoric and Early Iron Age sites (10000BC - 500BC), Upper Palaeolithic and Neolithic figures (10000BC - 6000BC) are based on the mammoth-bone dwelling rings at Mezhirich, Dobranichevka, Gontsy and Kirillovskaya (100 - 250 inhabitants) and the Dnieper-Donets cemeteries at Nikolskoye and Vovnigi (300 - 450 inhabitants) [@tolochko1972; @videiko2004]. Trypillia BII-CI figures (3600BC) follow geomagnetic house counts across the Cherkasy-Uman plateau between the Ros and the Southern Bug (Talianky at 450 ha with ~2,7k houses; Maidanetske at 200 ha with ~2,1k houses; Nebelivka at 260 ha with ~1,45k houses; and Dobrovody at 250 ha), assuming 75 - 80% of the houses were occupied at the same time by 5,5 - 6,5 persons per two-storey *ploshchadka* homestead [@videiko2004; @diachenko2012; @kruts1989]. Scythian forest-steppe hillfort and Greek colonial figures (500BC) follow excavated housing quarters at Belsk (Gelonus, 4,02k ha perimeter, 152,6 ha across the Western, Eastern and Kuzeminsk forts, 12k), Trakhtemyriv (500 ha, 4,5k), Motronyn (200 ha, 4k), Nemirov (110 ha, 4k) and the 50 ha stone-walled town of Olbia (15k) [@shramko1987; @kryzhitsky1999; @daragan2017].

For Kievan Rus fortified towns (*gorodishcha*) and suburbs (*posady*, 800AD - 1240AD), following P. P. Tolochko [@tolochko1983; @tolochko1989], A. V. Kuza [@kuza1989; @kuza1996] and M. A. Sahaydak [@sahaydak1991], towns are divided into the inner citadel (*detinets*), outer walled town (*okolny gorod*) and unfortified riverside craft suburbs (*posady* and *podol*). Inside the densely built *detinets* and *okolny gorod* ramparts, average homestead (*usadba*) plots measure 300 - 500 m² (20 - 25 homesteads per hectare at 5,5 - 6 persons per household, or 110 - 150 persons/ha). In outer *posad* quarters and the cavalry towns of the Porossia and Posullya frontier lines, wider courtyard plots (600 - 900 m²) give 70 - 110 persons/ha [@morgunov2003; @motsia2007].

For the Mongol conquest and late thirteenth-century recovery (1240AD - 1400AD), estimates reflect the 1239-1240AD destruction layers across Pereyaslavl, Posullya, Porossia and Kiev, John of Plano Carpini's 1246AD eyewitness report of ~200 surviving households in Kievan *Podol* (4k inhabitants in Kiev in 1250AD, recovering to 8,5k by 1300AD according to H. Yu. Ivakin) and the survival of the Drevlian Polesia and Bolokhov Land towns prior to Daniel of Galicia's 1257AD campaign [@ivakin1996; @dawson1955; @tomashevsky2008].
